analysis.body:
Defense is one of the most active sectors for AI procurement in the federal government, with documented spending concentrated in three functional areas: decision support, autonomous systems, and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance processing. The Defense Innovation Unit serves as the primary on-ramp through which commercial AI technology enters Department of Defense programs, maintaining public project listings that make its portfolio visible to outside researchers and vendors. Federal AI research organizations operating within the defense space are separately catalogued through government lab directories, and the Silicon Valley Defense Group, a nonprofit, publicly maps the commercial technology companies and private capital flows that are driving adoption across the national security market.

The full procurement record is traceable through publicly accessible federal systems. Contract opportunities and awards appear in SAM.gov, the government's official system of record for solicitations and vendor registrations. USAspending carries the downstream award data, built on the Federal Procurement Data System feed, which itself records DoD contract actions and vendor performance history at the transaction level. Govini, a defense-intelligence platform used inside the Department, builds decision science on top of that same record, producing public scorecards on critical-technology spending including AI and autonomy, and tracking supply-chain risk alongside vendor capability.

The existence of layered procurement infrastructure, from SAM.gov through FPDS to USAspending, reflects both the scale of activity and the compliance obligations that shape how vendors engage with this sector. Defense AI procurement carries strict requirements around security, supply-chain provenance, and vendor vetting that have no equivalent in commercial markets, and the data systems themselves are designed to enforce accountability at the transaction level. Janes and Forecast International maintain subscription databases covering contractors, programs, and procurement forecasts across the defense-industrial base, though the free federal sources provide a substantial foundation before subscription analysis is needed.

A reader evaluating whether to deploy in this space should understand that the commercial entry path runs through the Defense Innovation Unit rather than through conventional enterprise sales, that the full spending record is public and auditable by competitors as well as customers, and that supply-chain risk and critical-technology provenance are active screening criteria rather than background concerns. The procurement data is granular enough to support competitive intelligence before a single proposal is written, and the nonprofit and government sources together give a clear picture of where vendor activity and program investment are concentrating.
